modalities.name: Rough Draft Gestures
modalities.tagline: Let small body movements speak before you reach for words.
modalities.whatItIs: Rough Draft Gestures is a proposed practice in which small, unplanned movements count as part of how you sense a situation, a rough draft that comes before any words. You hold a life question lightly, let any urge to move show itself in a slow and small way, and only afterwards ask whether a word fits what moved.
modalities.coreIdea: The vague bodily sense of a situation sometimes shows up as an impulse to move, such as curling, pushing, reaching or trembling, before it shows up as words. Letting that impulse unfold gently, then naming it, may offer a fresh angle on something that feels stuck.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the basics from a teacher, you spend about ten minutes on gentle leg and hip exercises, then lie or sit for 20 minutes, alone or with a quiet partner nearby, and bring one situation to mind. When you notice an urge to move, you let it happen slowly and small, follow it until it stops, then repeat it even smaller to check whether it fits the situation, the way you would check a word, and wait to see whether a word or image comes. You can end at any time by opening your eyes, pressing your feet into the floor and looking around the room.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel a situation clearly in their body but go blank when asked to put it into words. Fans of body practices who want them linked to everyday questions may like it too.
modalities.cautions: The practice is untested and can still bring up strong feelings or memories, so keep movements small and stop whenever you choose. People with severe trauma, dissociation or psychosis should try it only with a qualified therapist, and anyone who is pregnant or has epilepsy, seizures or a recent injury, fracture or surgery should check with a doctor first.
modalities.tweet: New concept: Rough Draft Gestures. Bring a stuck situation to mind, let your body make the small move it wants (a curl, a push, a tremble), then see if a word fits. Made for people who feel things clearly but go blank when asked to explain them.

modalities.name: Witnessed Unbracing
modalities.tagline: Gentle shaking and loosening, with a guide who simply notices alongside you.
modalities.whatItIs: Witnessed Unbracing is a one-to-one concept in which a trained guide keeps you company while gentle shaking and loosening happen in your body. The guide does not steer or interpret but quietly names what they see, such as a breath deepening or a jaw letting go, so that long-held bracing is met with steady attention instead of being worked on.
modalities.coreIdea: Bracing that formed long ago may soften more readily when someone calmly notices it with you than when you push against it alone. Nothing is produced or forced; whatever the body does is simply accompanied.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a quiet room you spend about ten minutes on mild stretches and gentle leg exercises, then lie or sit while any trembling, sighing or loosening comes by itself, and the guide sits nearby and reflects back what they notice in a few plain words. Now and then they ask what you feel and where, and if a memory or emotion arrives you can name it, simply sense it or let it pass. Sessions last about an hour, weekly or every two weeks, and you can pause or stop at any moment.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry long-held tension and would rather be accompanied than do body work alone, especially those drawn to slow, presence-based coaching in which the body, not the story, leads.
modalities.cautions: As an untested concept it can stir old feelings or memories, so the guide needs to know when to pause and when to refer you to a trauma therapist. People with severe trauma, PTSD, dissociation, psychosis or suicidal thoughts should work with a licensed mental health professional rather than a coach, and anyone who is pregnant or has epilepsy, seizures or a recent injury, fracture or surgery should check with a doctor first.
modalities.tweet: An idea for anyone who has carried tension for years: Witnessed Unbracing. You lie down, let small shakes and sighs come by themselves, and a trained guide calmly notices them with you. No pushing, no analysis, just quiet company for whatever your body does.

modalities.name: Body Off Duty
modalities.tagline: A slow walk with one rule: stop managing your body.
modalities.whatItIs: Body Off Duty is an untested walking practice with a single rule: whenever you notice yourself managing your body, you stop. You walk slowly without correcting your posture, choosing a pace or holding anything in, and if the body wants to pause, stretch, sigh, shake out its arms or sit down, you let it.
modalities.coreIdea: Much everyday tension is quiet management, like holding the belly in, bracing the shoulders or trying to walk well, and dropping that effort may leave room for the body's own small unwinding movements, such as sighs, yawns, stretches and the odd tremble. Nothing has to happen, so an ordinary, unremarkable walk counts just as much.
modalities.whatYouDo: You set a timer for 20 to 30 minutes and walk slowly, alone, in a quiet park, garden or large room, with your phone away. Each time you catch an effort, such as straightening up, setting a pace, swinging your arms properly or trying to relax, you let that effort go and see what the body does next, whether that is drifting to a stop, stretching, sighing or carrying on. If it wants to sit or lie on the grass for a while, that is part of the practice too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are always holding themselves together and find even relaxation exercises effortful. Anyone who wants a body practice with almost no instructions could start here.
modalities.cautions: Nothing here has been studied, and with no anchor you may drift into worry or feel old emotions surface, so keep the first sessions short, choose a safe, familiar place and stop if it becomes too much. People with balance problems should walk where they can easily sit down, and people with severe trauma, dissociation or psychosis should try it only with guidance from a qualified therapist.
modalities.tweet: Body Off Duty, an untested idea: take a slow walk and drop every effort to manage your body. No standing up straight, no holding in. If it wants to stretch, sigh or stop, let it. For people who feel they are always holding themselves together.

modalities.name: Afterglow Absorption
modalities.tagline: Rest in the warm, loose feeling after gentle shaking until attention settles.
modalities.whatItIs: Afterglow Absorption imagines a concentration practice whose object is the warmth, looseness or tingling that can follow gentle tremor exercises. Instead of starting from a phrase or the breath, you start from a pleasant feeling the body has just produced and let attention gather around it.
modalities.coreIdea: Deep concentration practices often rest on a pleasant feeling, and many beginners struggle to find one while sitting still. A few minutes of gentle shaking may leave a ready-made one, which you then grow on purpose with steady, friendly attention.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn a short sequence of mild leg and hip stretches from a teacher, do it for about ten minutes, and let any gentle trembling run for a few minutes before lying still. For the next 20 minutes you rest attention on the most pleasant sensation you can find, such as warmth in the legs or a soft hum in the hands, and each time it fades you quietly return to it and let it spread without grasping. If it helps the feeling grow, you can add a silent wish such as 'may this body be at ease'.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who find it hard to locate a pleasant feeling in sitting practice, and people who want a calmer, more absorbing finish to body work. Those who like a clear sequence to follow will find one here.
modalities.cautions: Because this is an untested concept, keep sessions short at first: shaking can stir emotions or memories, and deep absorption can bring strong energy or unusual sensations. Anyone with a history of psychosis, mania, dissociation or severe trauma should talk to a clinician first, and anyone who is pregnant or has epilepsy, seizures or a recent injury, fracture or surgery should check with a doctor.
modalities.tweet: For meditators who can never find the 'pleasant feeling' they are told to rest on, a concept: Afterglow Absorption. Do a few gentle shaking exercises, then rest your attention on the warm, tingly calm that can follow and let it grow into deep focus.

modalities.name: Ripple by Ripple
modalities.tagline: Watch a gentle tremor closely to see how every sensation changes.
modalities.whatItIs: Ripple by Ripple is an idea for insight meditation with an unusual object: a mild, self-induced tremor, observed closely. Instead of letting the shaking run in the background, you watch it moment by moment and quietly label what you notice, such as pulse, flutter, warmth or stillness.
modalities.coreIdea: A tremor is a vivid stream of sensation that never holds still, which makes it an unusually clear place to see that experience keeps changing. Watching it with even, unreactive attention is meant to train both close noticing and the habit of not pushing sensations away.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning a short sequence of tiring leg exercises from a teacher, you lie down with bent knees and let a gentle tremor begin. In rounds of five minutes you note each change in a soft inner voice ('buzzing', 'spreading', 'fading'), then rest for a minute without noting, for three or four rounds. You keep the tremor mild by shifting your legs, and you finish by straightening them and noting the stillness that follows.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who find subtle sensations hard to follow and want a stronger, clearer object to study, and people who already do tremor exercises and want to give the shaking their full attention.
modalities.cautions: This pairing is untested, and both tremor work and intensive noting can bring up fear, strong emotions or old memories, so keep rounds short and stop by straightening your legs whenever you choose. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first, and anyone who is pregnant or has epilepsy, seizures or a recent injury, fracture or surgery should check with a doctor.
modalities.tweet: Experimental idea: Ripple by Ripple. Start a gentle leg tremor, then watch it closely and label each change: buzzing, spreading, fading. A vivid object for meditators, and a clear look at how every sensation comes and goes.

modalities.name: Hard Bout, Soft Landing
modalities.tagline: Hard bursts, then hands-off rests that let your body come down.
modalities.whatItIs: Hard Bout, Soft Landing turns the usual interval workout around: in this untested concept, the recovery is the main event. You alternate short, hard bouts of exercise with longer seated rests in which you leave your racing heart, heavy breathing and any shaking in your legs completely alone, instead of walking it off, stretching or using a breathing technique.
modalities.coreIdea: Going up into strong activation and coming back down, again and again, could build trust that a pounding heart and shaky legs settle by themselves. The hard bouts provide the surge, and the hands-off rest is where you practice not interfering.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a ten-minute warm-up you do five or six rounds of about one minute of hard effort, such as fast cycling or brisk stair climbing, at a level that is challenging but not all-out. Between rounds you walk for half a minute, then sit on the floor or a low bench with your back against a wall for about three minutes, hands open, watching your heartbeat and breathing slow down and leaving any trembling in your legs untouched. A few minutes of easy walking close the 35 to 40 minute session, done alone or with a coach twice a week.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy tough training but struggle to switch off afterwards, and anyone curious to see how their body settles after a surge when they stop managing it.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts strain the heart, so get medical advice first if you have heart problems, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, epilepsy or seizures, or a recent injury, fracture or surgery, or if you are pregnant or new to exercise, and add bouts gradually. Because the concept is untested, anyone whose racing heart tends to set off panic, or who has a history of trauma, should talk to a clinician before trying it and use it only with their guidance.
modalities.tweet: Proposed workout: Hard Bout, Soft Landing. One minute of hard effort, then sit against a wall and leave your pounding heart and shaky legs alone while they settle. Repeat. The rest is the real practice: noticing, in your body, that a big surge passes.

modalities.name: The Mistake Wiggle
modalities.tagline: A team ritual: shake out every mistake together, then play on.
modalities.whatItIs: The Mistake Wiggle is a proposed ritual that any recreational team can add to its games: after a dropped pass, a missed shot or a clumsy moment, the players nearby stop for a few seconds and shake out their arms, shoulders and legs together before play resumes. Unlike a private reset gesture, it is done with whoever is around, so a mistake becomes a shared, slightly silly moment instead of a lonely one.
modalities.coreIdea: Mistakes tend to linger in the body as tight shoulders and a held breath, and it is hard to stay clenched while loosely shaking, so a quick shake-out with teammates may make it easier to let a mistake go before it spreads into the next play. Doing it together makes it normal for anyone on the team to have a wobble.
modalities.whatYouDo: Before the season, the team agrees on the ritual and practices it in warm-ups: a three-second wiggle of the arms and legs, one long out-breath and a quick 'go'. During games anyone can start it after a mistake, their own or a teammate's, and whoever is nearby joins in while the rest of the game runs as usual. After each session the team spends a minute noticing whether mistakes felt any different, and drops or changes the ritual if it starts to feel forced.
modalities.whoItsFor: Recreational players who replay their mistakes for hours, and teams that want a lighter, kinder culture without changing the game itself.
modalities.cautions: Team sport brings injury risk, so warm up, keep play non-contact where possible, stop after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. The idea is untested, and the ritual should stay voluntary and playful, never a way to single out or tease the person who made the mistake.
modalities.tweet: Dropped a pass? In this new team ritual, The Mistake Wiggle, everyone nearby shakes out their arms and legs for three seconds, breathes out, and play resumes. Mistakes get let go on the spot, together. A lighter way to play if you replay every error. 🥏

modalities.name: Loose Like Laundry
modalities.tagline: An easy run where you let each footstep jiggle your whole body.
modalities.whatItIs: Loose Like Laundry is a proposed way of running at an easy, steady pace with an unusually soft, loose upper body, so that the small jolt of each footstep jiggles your shoulders, arms, hands and face like washing on a line. It borrows from tremor practice the habit of letting the body shake without controlling it, and finds that shaking in the ordinary rhythm of a run.
modalities.coreIdea: Shaking practices ask you to let movement pass through the body without steering it, and a steady run already provides a gentle, rhythmic shake with every step. Running loosely enough to feel it, instead of holding yourself tidy and upright, turns an ordinary run into long, rhythmic practice in not holding on.
modalities.whatYouDo: You run or jog alone for 30 to 45 minutes at a conversational pace on even ground, alternating five minutes of loose running with two or three minutes in your normal style. In the loose stretches you let your jaw go soft, your shoulders drop and your arms swing and flop, and you notice the jiggle travel up through your body with each step while your feet and knees keep their usual line. You finish by walking for five minutes and shaking your arms out once more before you stop.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners who finish even easy runs tight and hunched, and anyone who likes rhythm and routine and wants a low-cost practice that mixes fitness with loosening up.
modalities.cautions: As an untested concept it carries the usual running risks, so keep your feet and knees tracking normally, build up time gradually, take rest days and get medical advice first if you have heart disease, a recent injury or another medical condition. Running loosely on uneven ground raises the risk of a fall, so keep the loose stretches for flat, familiar routes.
modalities.tweet: For runners, a speculative idea: Loose Like Laundry. Drop your shoulders, let your jaw and arms go soft, and feel each footstep jiggle you from feet to face. Not faster, just looser. Worth a try if you finish even easy runs wound up tight.

modalities.name: Wobble Holds
modalities.tagline: Hold steady through the tremble instead of clenching against it.
modalities.whatItIs: Wobble Holds is an untested strength routine built on slow holds, such as wall sits, planks and split squats, kept going a little past the point where the muscles start to quiver. The aim is to stay steady and breathe slowly through the tremble rather than grip harder, so that the quiver becomes part of the exercise instead of an alarm.
modalities.coreIdea: Trembling under load is usually taken as a cue to clench or quit, while tremor practice lets shaking happen, and learning to stay steady while the muscles quiver could build both strength and a calmer response to feeling shaky. The quiver is read as information, not failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: Ideally after a few sessions with a coach to learn good form, you do four to six holds of 20 to 60 seconds, two or three times a week, choosing a load or position that brings a mild tremble near the end while you can still breathe easily. When the shaking starts you soften your face, breathe out slowly and hold for a few more seconds, then stand, walk a few steps and loosely shake out the worked muscles before the next hold. Each week you add a few seconds or a little load, keeping every hold well short of strain.
modalities.whoItsFor: People new to strength training who feel anxious when their body shakes, and lifters who want to practice staying calm under effort. Each hold can be timed, which appeals to people who like measurable progress.
modalities.cautions: Untested as a method, it also shares the risks of strength training: holding your breath under load spikes blood pressure, so breathe throughout and stop at any sharp pain, and get medical advice first if you have high blood pressure, heart or eye disease, epilepsy or seizures, or a recent injury, fracture or surgery, or if you are pregnant. Shaking can sometimes stir emotions or memories, so people with severe trauma or dissociation should explore it with a qualified practitioner.
modalities.tweet: Shaky muscles usually mean clench or quit. A new idea, Wobble Holds: hold a wall sit or plank until you start to quiver, then breathe slowly and stay steady. Rest, shake out, repeat. Practice for staying calm when your body shakes.

modalities.name: Take It From the Dog
modalities.tagline: Copy a calm dog's stretches and sighs, without a word spoken.
modalities.whatItIs: Take It From the Dog is an imagined wordless session, led by a professional with a calm, trained dog and its handler, in which you copy the relaxed things the dog does on its own: the long stretch after it gets up, the deep sigh as it settles, rolling onto its side. Like tremor practice, it stays with the body rather than with conversation, and the dog sets the example.
modalities.coreIdea: A relaxed animal stretches, sighs and settles without thinking about it, and copying those movements beside it may make it easier to let your own body unwind in small ways, with sighs, yawns, loosening and the occasional tremble. The dog is a companion and an example, never a tool, and it is never asked to perform.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a quiet room or garden you spend about 45 minutes with the facilitator, the handler and a calm dog, mostly in silence, walking a little together and then sitting or lying on mats near the dog. Whenever the dog stretches, sighs, settles or rolls over, the facilitator quietly points it out and you try your own version, such as a long full-body stretch, a slow, audible out-breath or curling up on your side. The session closes with a few minutes sitting beside the resting dog, a hand on its back if it is comfortable with that, noticing how your breathing compares with its own.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find talk-based approaches hard and feel more at ease around animals, and anyone who wants to learn simple, body-based ways of winding down in a warm, low-pressure setting.
modalities.cautions: This untested concept carries the usual risks of animal work, including allergies, fear of dogs, bites, scratches and infections, so contact is always optional, the dog must be trained, well cared for and free to move away, and the handler ends the session at any sign that the dog is uncomfortable. Strong feelings can surface even in quiet body work, so people with severe trauma, dissociation or a serious mental health condition should work with a licensed professional, and anyone who is pregnant or injured should adapt the stretches.
modalities.tweet: Dogs stretch, sigh and settle without a second thought. Take It From the Dog is a new concept: a quiet session with a calm trained dog where you copy its stretches and sighs, no talking needed. For animal lovers who find talking things through hard. 🐕

modalities.name: Breathing Alongside
modalities.tagline: Let a slow, counted breath keep company with a gentle tremor.
modalities.whatItIs: Breathing Alongside is a proposed sequence that alternates slow, breath-paced standing movements, which gently tire the thighs, with seated rounds in which you pair any mild leg tremor with slow, counted breathing. It borrows the way moving meditation forms pair the breath with each movement and applies it to a movement you do not choose.
modalities.coreIdea: Moving meditation coordinates the breath with movements you choose, and here the movement is involuntary, so the breath becomes a steady partner to something you cannot direct. Noticing how the tremor and a long out-breath meet, without forcing either, is meant to make the shaking feel held rather than random.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the sequence from a teacher, you alternate for about 30 minutes between three minutes of slow, deep sinking into the knees on each out-breath and rising on each in-breath, and three minutes sitting on a low stool with feet flat and knees bent. If a small tremor begins in your thighs while you sit, you breathe in for a count of four and out for a count of six alongside it, keeping it mild by moving your feet a little closer together or further apart. You finish by standing and walking slowly for a few minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like gentle, repeatable routines and enjoy breath work, and anyone who has tried tremor exercises and found the shaking hard to settle into. It suits people who would rather sit up than lie on the floor.
modalities.cautions: The sequence is untested, and slow counted breathing can leave some people light-headed, so breathe gently, return to normal breathing if you feel dizzy and keep rounds short at first. Anyone with a history of psychosis, severe trauma or dissociation should get medical advice and learn from an experienced teacher, and anyone who is pregnant or has epilepsy, seizures or a recent injury, fracture or surgery should check with a doctor first.
modalities.tweet: Breath-work fans, here's an idea: Breathing Alongside. Slow, deep knee bends can set off a gentle leg tremor, then, sitting, you breathe in for four and out for six alongside it, letting the breath keep the shaking company. Calm, counted and seated.

modalities.name: Loosen Then Linger
modalities.tagline: A friendly meetup where the body loosens first and talking is optional.
modalities.whatItIs: Loosen Then Linger is a concept for a social gathering that opens with about 25 minutes of gentle, shared movement (shaking out the arms and legs, stretching and a slow stroll around the block or garden) and then moves into tea and unhurried company. Conversation is welcome but never required, so the body does the first part of the connecting.
modalities.coreIdea: Social nerves live partly in the body, and loosening up side by side may lower the guard more easily than small talk can. Once people feel a bit looser and a bit sillier together, staying to chat can feel easier.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five to twelve friends or neighbors meet weekly in a living room, garden or community space, where a volunteer host leads an easy, playful shake-out and stretch, followed by a slow walk together of about 15 minutes. Then everyone lingers over tea or a simple snack for as long as they like, chatting or just sitting together. There are no rounds, no sharing exercises and no pressure to talk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want more company but find talk-heavy socializing tense or tiring. Groups of friends looking for a regular ritual that feels relaxed rather than performed could adopt it too.
modalities.cautions: Untested as a format, it should keep all movement gentle and optional, and anyone who is pregnant or has a recent injury or heart problems should adapt or skip it. If social situations bring intense fear or a low mood that does not lift, talk to a doctor or therapist, and step back from any group that feels unsafe or unkind.
modalities.tweet: Want company but dread small talk? Loosen Then Linger is a new idea: friends meet, shake out, stretch and stroll together, then stay for tea. Talking is optional. Let your body break the ice first.

modalities.name: Small Arrivals
modalities.tagline: After each steep bit of trail, stop and let your legs settle.
modalities.whatItIs: Small Arrivals is a new idea for hiking in which the trail sets the rhythm: after every steep climb, scramble or nervy crossing, you stop at a safe spot for a minute or two and let your body settle before you walk on. You stand with soft knees or sit on a rock, let any trembling in your legs come and go, and take in the view, the wind and the sounds around you.
modalities.coreIdea: Hiking is full of small, real challenges that leave the legs shaky and the heart quick, and instead of pushing straight on you give each one a still moment, borrowing tremor practice's habit of letting shakiness run its course. The pauses turn one long effort into a series of small arrivals.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose a familiar route with a few steep or rocky sections, alone or with a friend, and walk it at your own pace for one to three hours. After each challenging stretch you stop somewhere flat and safe, stand with soft knees or sit down, let your breathing and any shaking in your legs settle without hurrying them, and spend that minute looking and listening before you set off again. At the top or the halfway point you take a longer rest, with water and something to eat.
modalities.whoItsFor: Walkers who tend to push on without a break and arrive home more wound up than when they left, and anyone who wants a simple outdoor practice that combines effort, rest and the senses.
modalities.cautions: Nothing here has been tested, and hiking brings slips, sprains, weather changes, ticks and the risk of getting lost, so pick a known route, check the forecast, carry water, tell someone where you are going and only pause where you cannot fall. Get medical advice before steep climbs if you have heart problems, check with a doctor first if you are pregnant or have epilepsy, seizures or a recent injury, fracture or surgery, and explore the trembling with a qualified practitioner if you have severe trauma or dissociation.
modalities.tweet: Walkers, a proposal: Small Arrivals. After every steep or tricky bit of trail, stop somewhere safe, let your legs shake and your breath settle, and take in the view before walking on. Effort, then stillness, all the way up. 🌄

modalities.name: Outside Anchors
modalities.tagline: Shift between your trembling legs and the room's sounds and textures.
modalities.whatItIs: Outside Anchors is a self-led concept that pairs a mild leg tremor with deliberate shifts of attention between the inside of the body and the world outside it. When the trembling feels strong, you turn toward sounds, light and the texture of the floor under your hands, and when it feels faint, you turn back in.
modalities.coreIdea: Attention to the room may make strong inner sensations feel less overwhelming, and attention to the body may bring faint ones into view. Moving between the two on purpose is meant to keep the experience at a comfortable level and anchored in the present.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once you have learned a few gentle tiring leg exercises from a teacher, you do them in a room you know well, then sit on the floor with your back against a wall and knees bent, and let a small tremor begin for 15 to 20 minutes. Every couple of minutes, or whenever it feels like too much, you open your eyes and name three things you can hear, see or feel against your skin, letting the tremor carry on in the background, and you turn your attention inside again once you feel settled. You end by straightening your legs, sitting quietly for a minute and looking around the room.
modalities.whoItsFor: People curious about tremor exercises who worry they might feel too intense, and anyone who wants a practical skill for staying grounded. Sensory mindfulness fans looking for a more physical version may like it.
modalities.cautions: The approach is untested, and heightened sensitivity, fear or old memories can still surface, so keep the freedom to stop by straightening your legs or getting up. People with severe trauma, PTSD, dissociation or psychosis should try it only with a qualified therapist, and anyone who is pregnant or has epilepsy, seizures or a recent injury, fracture or surgery should check with a doctor first.
modalities.tweet: Worried that trembling exercises might feel like too much? Outside Anchors is a proposed practice: let your legs gently tremble, and when it gets intense, open your eyes and name three sounds or textures around you. Inside, outside, back again.

modalities.name: Duet for Trembling Legs
modalities.tagline: A musician plays along with your tremor, following where it goes.
modalities.whatItIs: Duet for Trembling Legs imagines a one-to-one session in which a music facilitator improvises softly on a hand drum, guitar or keyboard, following the speed and strength of a gentle tremor running through your legs. Instead of moving to music, you hear your body's own movement answered in sound, and later the musician slows and quiets the music to see whether the tremor follows.
modalities.coreIdea: Involuntary shaking can feel odd or lonely, and hearing a musician answer it in real time may make it feel companionable instead. Because the music follows the body first, any later invitation to slow down comes from a partner that has been listening, not from a beat imposed from outside.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a few gentle tiring leg exercises, you sit or lie in whatever position is comfortable while a mild tremor begins, and the facilitator, sitting nearby, matches its pace and strength with quiet sounds for about 20 minutes. Now and then they slow or soften the music, and you notice whether the shaking follows, changes or carries on as before, knowing you can change position or stop at any moment. Afterwards you can talk briefly about it or simply sit with a last few notes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are curious about tremor exercises but find them strange or lonely on their own, and music lovers who would like a body practice that feels like a conversation.
modalities.cautions: The idea is untested, and both music and trembling can stir strong feelings or memories, so keep the volume low, agree on a stop signal beforehand and stop whenever you wish. People with severe trauma, dissociation or psychosis should try it only with a qualified therapist, and anyone who is pregnant or has epilepsy, seizures or a recent injury, fracture or surgery should check with a doctor first.
modalities.tweet: Usually you move to music. Here the music moves to you. New concept: Duet for Trembling Legs. Gentle exercises invite a mild leg tremor, a musician plays along with it, then slowly quiets to see if your body follows. Solo body work, made less lonely.

modalities.name: The Truest Sentence
modalities.tagline: Keep refining one sentence about your life until your whole body agrees.
modalities.whatItIs: The Truest Sentence is a proposed one-to-one practice in which you and a trained guide work on a single sentence about where you are in your life. You say it, sense whether it rings true in your body and revise it slowly until it fits, and each truer version may uncover something that was not visible before.
modalities.coreIdea: When words fit what you feel, the body often responds with a small sense of relief or recognition, and following that response one sentence at a time can lead gently beneath the surface. The work is about uncovering what is already true, not about improving yourself.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a 60-minute session, in person or online, you begin with a rough sentence such as 'I am stuck at work', and the guide repeats it back slowly so you can sense whether it fits. Each time something feels off you adjust it, perhaps to 'part of me is afraid to want more', while the guide reflects your words and tone without adding ideas of their own. Sessions run every week or two, and between them you can practice alone by writing a sentence, pausing and sensing before you change it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel stuck or self-critical, are not in crisis, and want a slow, precise way of finding out what they really feel. Word lovers who want their words to come from somewhere deeper than analysis may be drawn to it.
modalities.cautions: As an untested concept it can still stir strong feelings or old memories when a sentence rings true, so the guide should know when to pause and when to refer you to a therapist. People with severe depression, PTSD, psychosis, suicidal thoughts or another serious mental health condition should work with a licensed mental health professional.
modalities.tweet: What if you kept rewriting one sentence about your life until your body said 'yes, that's it'? New concept: The Truest Sentence. A guide reflects it back, you adjust, and each truer version shows you a little more. For people who feel stuck and want clarity.

modalities.name: Sitting Ajar
modalities.tagline: Leave room for a feeling to arrive, and ask nothing of it.
modalities.whatItIs: Sitting Ajar is an untested meditation in which you leave yourself slightly open, like a door ajar, for a vague, whole-body sense of something in your life, and do nothing to it if it shows up. There is no searching for words, no questioning and no goal of change, and if no such sense comes, you simply sit.
modalities.coreIdea: Many inner practices ask a feeling for something, such as a name, a message or a next step, and that asking can quietly turn into pressure. Here the only job is to keep company with whatever arrives, letting any shift happen by itself or not at all.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit comfortably for 15 to 25 minutes, alone, and begin by noticing how your body feels as a whole. If a sense of a situation forms, such as a heaviness about a friendship or a flutter about a decision, you let it be there without naming or questioning it, and if you catch yourself trying to understand or change it, you drop the effort. When the time ends you can jot down anything that stood out, or nothing.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find guided inner work too effortful or goal-driven, and those who already know their inner life well and want to rest with it. Anyone who dislikes detailed instructions will find almost none.
modalities.cautions: Because it is untested and has no anchor, you may drift, doze or slide into worry, and painful feelings or memories can surface, so keep sessions short and stop if it becomes distressing. People with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or a current crisis should practice with a qualified teacher or therapist.
modalities.tweet: A gentle new idea: Sitting Ajar. Sit quietly and leave room for a feeling about your life to show up. If it comes, keep it company without analyzing it or asking anything of it. If it doesn't, just sit. For anyone tired of trying hard at inner work.

modalities.name: Wishes for the Unnamed
modalities.tagline: Offer kind wishes to your own unclear moods, from easy to hard.
modalities.whatItIs: Wishes for the Unnamed sketches a meditation that offers loving-kindness not to people but to your own inner states: the vague, hard-to-name feelings in the body that come with a situation. Following a set order, you move from a pleasant inner state to a neutral one to a difficult one, offering each a quiet, kind wish.
modalities.coreIdea: Kindness practice usually travels outward through a widening circle of people, but the same circle can be turned toward the moods and murky feelings inside you. Meeting an unclear inner state with goodwill, instead of trying to decode it, may make it easier to stay with.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the steps from a teacher or a recording, you sit for 20 to 30 minutes and first find a pleasant inner state, perhaps a lightness in the chest, silently offering it a wish such as 'may you be at ease' until a warm feeling grows. Then you find a neutral state and offer it the same wish, and finally a difficult one, like a tight knot about a conflict, putting the wish in whatever words feel genuine. If the warmth deepens into steady calm, you rest there for a while before opening your eyes.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are hard on their own feelings and want a structured way to meet them more kindly. Loving-kindness practitioners who want the practice to reach the moods they usually push away may like it.
modalities.cautions: This is untested, and wishing yourself well can stir grief, anger or a sense of unworthiness, so begin with easy states, keep sessions short and stop if it becomes distressing. Anyone with a history of psychosis, mania, dissociation or severe trauma should talk to a clinician before practicing deeply or for long periods.
modalities.tweet: Imagine loving-kindness meditation aimed at your own moods. That's the new concept of Wishes for the Unnamed: offer kind wishes to a pleasant feeling, then a neutral one, then the knot you usually avoid. For people who are hard on their own feelings.

modalities.name: Knot Into Threads
modalities.tagline: See a heavy feeling as many small sensations, always changing.
modalities.whatItIs: Knot Into Threads is a proposed sitting practice that moves between two ways of meeting the vague bodily feel of a problem: as one heavy whole, and as many small sensations that arise and pass. You sense the whole, look closely at its threads, then sense the whole again and notice how it has changed.
modalities.coreIdea: A stuck situation often feels like one solid knot in the body, yet close attention tends to reveal tightness, heat, pulsing and pressure that keep shifting. Seeing the knot as threads in motion, then returning to the whole, may loosen the sense that the problem is solid and permanent.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning basic noting from a meditation teacher, you sit for about 30 minutes in three or four rounds, each beginning with a minute or two of sensing the overall feel of one situation in your body. Then for about five minutes you look closely at the sensations that make it up, softly noting 'tight', 'warm', 'pulsing' or 'fading', before widening again to sense the whole and noticing whether it feels any different. You keep a calm, even attention throughout and end with a few breaths of open awareness.
modalities.whoItsFor: People weighed down by a problem that seems solid and unchanging, and meditators who want a structured way to bring insight practice closer to everyday life.
modalities.cautions: The practice is untested, and close attention to difficult feelings can bring up fear, panic or old memories, so keep rounds short and switch to open eyes and steady breathing if it becomes too much. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or a current crisis should talk to a clinician first and avoid long, intensive sessions.
modalities.tweet: A proposed meditation: Knot Into Threads. Feel the heavy knot a problem makes in your body, then look closely: tightness, heat, pulsing, all shifting. Then feel the whole again. For anyone carrying something that feels solid and permanent.

modalities.name: Hearing Out the Quit
modalities.tagline: In hard intervals, listen to the urge to stop before deciding.
modalities.whatItIs: Hearing Out the Quit is an idea for interval training in which the urge to stop becomes something to listen to, rather than something to obey or override. During each hard bout you notice how the urge feels in your body, give it a word, and then choose freely whether to ease off or carry on.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people either push through every signal or stop at the first one, and both habits skip the moment of actually listening. Sensing what a 'quit' feels like and what it seems to be about could build a more honest, trusting relationship with your own limits.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a ten-minute warm-up you do six to eight bouts of about one minute at a brisk, fairly hard but not all-out effort, with two minutes of easy movement between them, on a bike, a rower or a hill. When the urge to stop appears, you notice where it lives in your body and what word fits it, such as 'scared', 'bored' or 'done', and then decide whether to ease off, slow down or finish the bout. Afterwards you take a minute to note which kinds of 'quit' you trusted and how that felt.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tend to overdo things or give up early, in exercise and elsewhere, and want to listen to themselves more fairly. Interval fans get a familiar structure with a new layer.
modalities.cautions: Untested as a method, it still puts strain on the heart, so get medical advice first if you have heart problems, chest pain, fainting or high blood pressure, or are pregnant, then build up gradually and always stop for pain, dizziness or chest discomfort. On any given day the listening part is optional, and when in doubt, ease off.
modalities.tweet: New idea for interval training: Hearing Out the Quit. When the urge to stop shows up, notice how it feels and give it a word (scared, bored, done) before you choose. Pain or dizziness always means stop. For people who always push through, or bail early.

modalities.name: Playing on a Hunch
modalities.tagline: Find an image for how the game feels, then play from it.
modalities.whatItIs: Playing on a Hunch is a proposed format for gentle team games in which short spells of play alternate with quick pauses where everyone senses how the team's play feels as a whole, beyond tactics or the score. The group settles on one shared image for that feeling, such as 'scattered birds' or 'wading through mud', and lets the next spell grow out of it, for example by asking what the scattered birds would need to fly as a flock.
modalities.coreIdea: A team often has a shared, wordless sense of how a game is going before anyone can explain it, and giving that sense an image may open up changes that tactics talk misses. The image is checked against everyone's feel for the game and dropped if it does not fit.
modalities.whatYouDo: Eight to twelve people play a friendly, non-contact game, such as a disc or ball game at an easy jog with walking allowed, in spells of about ten minutes. In each one-minute pause, players stand in a loose circle, close their eyes for a breath or two to sense how the last spell felt, and call out words or images until one fits for most of the group, then start the next spell with that image in mind. A volunteer keeps time, and after the last spell the group picks one image for the whole session to remember next week.
modalities.whoItsFor: Players who love the social side of sport and want a more playful, intuitive way of improving together, and groups who find tactics talk dry. It may also suit people who want to practice noticing and naming feelings in an active, low-pressure setting.
modalities.cautions: The format is untested, and even easy games bring risks of sprains, collisions and falls, so warm up, keep it non-contact, stop after any knock to the head and check with a doctor first if you have heart or joint problems. Images should describe the play, never individual players, and anyone can pass during the pauses.
modalities.tweet: Pickup game idea: Playing on a Hunch. Every ten minutes the team pauses, senses how the play feels as a whole and finds an image for it ('scattered birds'), then plays the next spell from it. For groups who find tactics talk dry.

modalities.name: Pace of the Problem
modalities.tagline: Move at your problem's pace, then find one you can keep.
modalities.whatItIs: Pace of the Problem is a walking concept built on one question: what pace does a current situation feel like in your body? You start by moving at that pace, whether frantic or dragging, then shift gradually toward a pace you could keep up for a long time, noticing how the situation feels as you do.
modalities.coreIdea: Situations can have a felt tempo, such as rushed, stalled or heavy, and the body can try out a different tempo before the mind knows how. Finding a steady, sustainable pace physically may hint at what a sustainable pace for the situation itself could be.
modalities.whatYouDo: You head out alone for 30 to 40 minutes and bring one situation to mind, such as a project or a strained relationship. For the first few minutes you move at the pace it feels like, perhaps a hurried half-jog or a heavy trudge, then ease step by step into a brisk, easy walk you could keep up for an hour while chatting, and stay there. Every ten minutes you check how the situation feels now and what word fits, and you finish with a slow stroll and a short note of anything you noticed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel rushed or stuck in some part of life and want to think it through with their body rather than in circles. Walkers who like a solo routine with a purpose are a good match.
modalities.cautions: Since the idea is untested, build up time gradually, keep the hurried part brief and gentle, and get medical advice first if you have heart disease or another medical condition. Turning toward a hard situation can stir strong feelings, so people in crisis or with severe trauma should use it with a qualified therapist rather than alone.
modalities.tweet: Thought experiment: what pace does your problem feel like? In Pace of the Problem you walk at that pace, frantic or dragging, then ease into one you could keep for an hour, and notice how the problem feels now. For people stuck in a rush, or a rut.

modalities.name: Strength on Loan
modalities.tagline: Train until you feel capable, then bring that feeling to a problem.
modalities.whatItIs: Strength on Loan is a proposed strength routine at light to moderate effort in which each set ends with a short pause to sense what being capable feels like in the body. Once that feeling is clear, you bring a stuck situation to mind and sense it from inside the capable body, as if borrowing the strength for it.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing a movement you could not manage a few weeks ago can give the body concrete, felt proof of 'I can', and that feeling may carry over to a situation where you feel small or stuck. The exercises build the feeling, and the pause lets you notice it and put it to use.
modalities.whatYouDo: Two or three times a week, after learning good technique, you do three or four simple exercises, such as slow bodyweight squats, wall push-ups and band rows, one or two sets each, at an effort that feels steady rather than hard. After each set you stand still for 30 seconds, notice where capability shows up in your body, such as steady legs or a broad chest, and find a word for it, like 'solid' or 'rooted'. At the end you hold one stuck situation in mind for a minute while standing in that feeling, and note what looks different from there.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel small or powerless in some situation and want a physical, step-by-step way to feel more capable, especially if they like measurable progress and simple routines.
modalities.cautions: The routine is untested: build up slowly, breathe out during effort instead of holding your breath, and get medical advice before starting if you have high blood pressure, heart or eye disease, or are pregnant. If a focus on size or appearance starts to take over, or the situation you bring to mind feels overwhelming, talk to a professional.
modalities.tweet: Strength on Loan, a new idea: after each easy set of squats or push-ups, pause and feel what 'I can' feels like in your legs and chest. Then bring to mind a situation where you feel small, from inside that feeling. Strength you can borrow.

modalities.name: A Listener With Fur
modalities.tagline: Let a calm dog's company be your safe base for exploring feelings.
modalities.whatItIs: A Listener With Fur is a new concept for a session in which the feeling of sitting with a calm, trained therapy dog becomes a home base for exploring something unclear inside. You first sense how the dog's company feels in your body and find a word for it, then explore a harder feeling in small steps, coming back to that home base whenever you need to.
modalities.coreIdea: Exploring a vague, uncomfortable feeling may be easier with somewhere safe inside to return to, and the warmth and steady breathing of a calm animal can make that safe place easy to find. The dog listens without judging, interrupting or advising, but the main thing it offers is a felt sense of steadiness you can come back to.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a quiet room you sit next to the dog for about 45 minutes, with a hand on its fur if you both want that, while a professional and the handler stay nearby. For the first few minutes you notice how being with the dog feels in your body, perhaps 'warm and slow', then you bring a situation to mind, sense it for a minute or two and tell the dog about it, out loud or silently. Whenever it feels like too much, you shift back to the dog's warmth and breathing and to your word for it until you feel settled, then decide whether to go on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to open up to another person but feel at ease with animals. Anyone who wants to explore feelings without the pressure of being watched or advised might prefer it.
modalities.cautions: Like all animal work, this untested idea brings risks of allergies, fear of dogs, bites, scratches and infections, so contact is always optional, the dog must be trained and well cared for, and the handler ends the session if it shows signs of stress. Strong feelings can surface, so people with severe trauma, dissociation, psychosis or a current crisis should work with a licensed mental health professional who offers animal-assisted sessions.
modalities.tweet: No judgment, no advice, just a warm, breathing listener. In A Listener With Fur, a new concept, you first notice how a calm therapy dog's company feels in your body, then explore something hard, coming back to that warmth whenever you need it.

modalities.name: Spacious Arms
modalities.tagline: Slow movements that make space around a difficult feeling.
modalities.whatItIs: Spacious Arms is a proposed sequence of slow movements in which each gesture is meant to make physical space around a feeling you are carrying. You locate where a difficult feeling sits, such as a tight chest or a heavy belly, then move your arms and breath slowly around that area, widening, lifting and opening, as if giving the feeling more room.
modalities.coreIdea: A feeling with room around it may be easier to stay with than one you are pressed up against, and slow, open movement may let the body sense that room directly. The aim is not to push the feeling away but to stand beside it with more space.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn five slow movements from a teacher, such as widening the arms around the chest on an in-breath or floating the hands forward from the belly on an out-breath, and practice them standing or seated for about 20 minutes, alone or in a small group. Before you start, you find where a feeling sits and choose the movements that open space around that place. After every few repetitions you pause, sense whether the feeling has more room, and let a word or image come if one fits.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel crowded or swamped by a feeling and want a calm, physical way to give it space, and anyone who likes gentle, repeatable movement and quiet attention.
modalities.cautions: This is untested, and turning toward a difficult feeling can bring up strong emotions or memories, so go slowly and stop if it becomes distressing. Anyone with a history of psychosis, severe trauma or dissociation should get advice from a clinician and learn with an experienced teacher, and people with injuries should adapt the movements.
modalities.tweet: When a feeling crowds you, give it room. That's the concept behind Spacious Arms: find where it sits, say a tight chest, and move your arms slowly and widely around that spot with your breath. Not pushing it away, just keeping it company with more space.

modalities.name: Social Aftertaste
modalities.tagline: Notice which company warms you, then plan more of it.
modalities.whatItIs: Social Aftertaste is a simple, untested habit that pairs regular social contact with a short check of the aftertaste each meeting leaves in your body. Over weeks, these quick impressions (lighter, warm, flat or tense) become a rough guide to the kinds of people, places and formats that suit you, so you can plan more of them.
modalities.coreIdea: The body may register whether a connection feels nourishing before the mind has an opinion, and noticing that gently can steer a social life toward more of what works rather than toward less contact. A flat or tense evening is usually read as information about the setting, such as a loud bar or a big group, not as a verdict on a person.
modalities.whatYouDo: Each week you plan a few contacts you can repeat, such as a call with a friend, a club meeting or a walk with a neighbor, and go to them as usual. Afterwards you take two minutes alone to notice how your body feels, find one word or image for it, and note it with a word about the setting. Once a month you look back, plan more of what felt warm, try a different format for what felt flat, such as a walk instead of a party, and add one new contact if your notes look thin.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who want a fuller social life but are not sure where to start, and people rebuilding a social circle after a move, breakup or loss. The habit is light and self-led, so it fits a busy week.
modalities.cautions: The practice is untested and is meant for adding and adjusting contact, not for cutting people off: if most meetings feel tense or flat, or you notice yourself pulling away, that is a reason to talk to someone you trust or a professional rather than to see people less. Step back only from contact that is hostile, controlling or abusive, and if social situations bring intense fear, panic or persistent low mood, talk to a doctor or therapist.
modalities.tweet: What aftertaste does each meetup leave? A new idea, Social Aftertaste: after each coffee, call or club night, take two minutes to notice how your body feels and jot down one word. Then plan more of what felt good. Handy when you're rebuilding a social life.

modalities.name: Waystone Walk
modalities.tagline: Set your worries down along the trail, then decide which to collect.
modalities.whatItIs: Waystone Walk is an idea for an out-and-back nature walk in which you set each current concern down, in your mind, at a landmark along the way. You walk on with lighter, open attention to the landscape, and on the return you pass each landmark and sense whether you want to pick that concern back up, and how it feels now.
modalities.coreIdea: Setting concerns aside one by one can make space to breathe, and a trail gives each one a real place to wait. Walking back past them after time among trees or water offers a fresh, gentler chance to sense what each one needs.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose a familiar path of 20 to 40 minutes each way, alone or with a quiet companion, and as you walk out you pause at a rock, tree or bend for each concern that comes to mind, sense how it feels in your body and leave it there. Once your concerns are set down, you walk on slowly with your phone away, taking in sights, sounds and smells. On the way back you stop briefly at each landmark, notice how that concern feels now, and choose whether to take it home, leave it for another day or simply notice it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who carry many worries at once and want a calm, simple way to sort through them outdoors. Walkers who prefer a light structure to a strict method may enjoy it.
modalities.cautions: The walk is untested as a practice, and outdoor walks bring slips, weather changes, ticks and the risk of getting lost, so choose a known route, check the weather and tell someone where you are going. If a concern feels overwhelming or low mood persists, talk to a doctor or therapist instead of carrying it alone.
modalities.tweet: Untested but simple: Waystone Walk. On the way out, 'leave' each worry at a rock or tree along the trail. Walk on and take in the view. On the way back, stop at each one and decide whether to pick it up. Try it when you're carrying too many worries at once.

modalities.name: Start With a Pebble
modalities.tagline: Learn to notice subtle inner feelings using a pebble, tea or sound.
modalities.whatItIs: Start With a Pebble is a beginner's concept for learning to notice the subtle, whole-body feel of something, using simple sensory objects before turning to harder life questions. You give full attention to a pebble, a cup of tea or a piece of music, first to its plain sensations and then to the overall feel it leaves in you, and only then look for a word.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people find the vague bodily feel of a problem hard to notice at first, but even a smooth stone may leave a quiet overall feel that is easier and safer to practice on. Training on small, neutral things is meant to build the skill before it is needed for bigger ones.
modalities.whatYouDo: For about 15 minutes a day, you choose one object or sound, such as a cool pebble, a warm mug or a short piece of music, and spend a few minutes on its plain sensations: weight, texture, temperature or tone. Then you set it down, notice the overall feel it leaves in your body, and wait for a word or image that fits, checking it once or twice. After a week or two you can try the same steps with a mild everyday situation.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have tried inner-awareness practices and found the bodily feel of a problem hard to find, and anyone who wants a gentle, low-stakes, hands-on way to start.
modalities.cautions: Although untested and mostly gentle, sensory attention can sometimes bring up unexpected feelings or memories, so keep the freedom to stop. People with severe trauma, dissociation or psychosis should practice with a qualified teacher or therapist.
modalities.tweet: Find it hard to sense what you feel? New concept: Start With a Pebble. Hold a pebble or a warm mug, notice its weight and texture, then the overall feel it leaves in you, and find a word for it. Practice on small things before the big ones.

modalities.name: Spoken Liner Notes
modalities.tagline: Bring a song that matches how you feel, then speak from it.
modalities.whatItIs: Spoken Liner Notes is a peer-group idea in which each person brings a piece of music that matches how some part of their life feels right now, especially the part that is hard to put into words. The group listens together in silence, and then that person speaks a few sentences from the feeling the music holds, like liner notes for their own week, while the others simply listen.
modalities.coreIdea: Music can carry a feeling before we have words for it, and letting others hear that feeling first may make the words easier to find. The song works as a bridge from a wordless feeling to a few honest sentences.
modalities.whatYouDo: Three to six friends or peers meet every week or two for about 90 minutes, with one person acting as a light host. In turn, each plays a track of up to four minutes while everyone listens with eyes closed, and then the person who chose it pauses, notices how the music and the situation feel in their body, and says whatever comes while the others listen without advice or comment. A shared silence of a few breaths closes each turn before the next song begins.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel things strongly through music but struggle to describe them, and friends who want a deeper but still relaxed way of being together. Anyone who would rather share a song than a speech is welcome.
modalities.cautions: This peer format is untested, and music can stir strong feelings or deepen a low mood, so choose tracks that feel safe to share, keep the volume moderate and let anyone pass. It is not therapy, so if low mood persists or something painful comes up, talk to a qualified professional or a credentialed music therapist.
modalities.tweet: A new idea for friends who love music: Spoken Liner Notes. Each person brings a track that sounds like something they can't put into words. Everyone listens in silence, then they speak a few sentences from that feeling. No advice, just listening. 🎧

modalities.name: Nobody Needs Anything
modalities.tagline: Sit in quiet company with a guide, with nothing to achieve.
modalities.whatItIs: Nobody Needs Anything pictures a one-to-one session in which a trained guide and a client sit together, mostly in silence, with no goal of solving, improving or exploring anything. The guide offers only steady, warm presence, and now and then a short invitation to let go of an effort they notice.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting go of control can be easier in good company than alone, and sitting with someone who wants nothing from you may leave room for whatever is already there to show itself. Old feelings that surface are met with the same unhurried acceptance as the quiet.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sessions last about an hour, in person or by video, every week or two. You and the guide sit comfortably and you let whatever happens happen (thoughts, sleepiness, feelings or calm), and if you notice yourself trying to have a good session you drop the effort, while the guide may softly name such moments or ask what is here now. In the last ten minutes you can say a few words about what it was like, or nothing at all.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who are tired of working on themselves and want space simply to be, in steady company. Those who are not in crisis and find meditating alone lonely or effortful may like it most.
modalities.cautions: As an untested concept, open and unstructured sitting can bring up difficult emotions or memories, so the guide should know how to pause a session and when to refer you to a mental health professional. People with severe depression, trauma, psychosis, dissociation or suicidal thoughts should work with a licensed clinician rather than a coach.
modalities.tweet: Tired of working on yourself? Here's a concept: Nobody Needs Anything. You sit with a trained guide, mostly in silence, with nothing to solve or improve. If you catch yourself trying, you let it go. A quiet hour with nothing to achieve.
